target: Os parci di fan hyn, efallai y cei di ddirwy.
english: If you park here, you might get a fine.
tip: ‘cei di’ is the future of ‘cael’, meaning you will get. So ‘cei di ddirwy’ means you'll get a fine, not one you already got.

target: Mae'r jig-so yn anodd iawn i'w gwblhau.
english: The jigsaw is very difficult to complete.
tip: ‘i'w gwblhau’ means to complete it. The ‘'w’ packs it in before the verb, so the noun isn't repeated.

target: Mae'r modrwy briodas yn symbol o gariad.
english: The wedding ring is a symbol of love.
tip: After ‘o’ (of), the next word softens: ‘cariad’ becomes ‘gariad’, giving ‘symbol o gariad’.

target: Aeth Owain i'r siop a phrynu llaeth.
english: Owain went to the shop and bought some milk.
tip: ‘a’ (and) changes the start of the next verb: ‘prynu’ becomes ‘phrynu’. ‘aeth Owain... a phrynu’ = went and bought.

target: Mae'r gwisgoedd yn cael eu gwnïo â llaw.
english: The costumes are sewn by hand.
tip: ‘cael’ + ‘eu’ + a verb says something is done to it: ‘cael eu gwnïo’ = are sewn. ‘eu’ points back to ‘gwisgoedd’, the costumes.

target: Roeddwn i'n darllen llyfr pan aeth y trydan.
english: I was reading a book when the power went out.
tip: ‘roeddwn i'n’ + a verb sets the background; a short past-tense verb cuts in: ‘darllen... pan aeth’ = reading when it went out.

target: Rwyt ti'n gwneud gwahaniaeth go iawn i'r gymuned hon.
english: You make a real difference to this community.
tip: ‘hon’ means this for feminine nouns. ‘cymuned’ is feminine, so it's ‘i'r gymuned hon’. A masculine noun would take ‘hwn’.

target: Es i â'r ci am dro yn y goedwig.
english: I took the dog for a walk in the woods.
tip: ‘mynd â’ means to take along: ‘es i â'r ci am dro’ = I took the dog for a walk, literally went with the dog.

target: Bwytaodd y plant yr holl gacen heb iddo sylwi nes ei bod yn rhy hwyr.
english: The children ate all the cake without him noticing until it was too late.
tip: ‘heb i’ + a person means without them doing something: ‘heb iddo sylwi’ = without him noticing.

target: Ffeindiodd Catrin fadarch a pherlysiau ffres yn y farchnad cyn iddi goginio swper yn y gegin.
english: Catrin found fresh mushrooms and herbs in the market before she cooked supper in the kitchen.
tip: ‘cyn i’ + a person softens the verb: ‘coginio’ becomes ‘goginio’. ‘cyn iddi goginio’ = before she cooked.

target: Mae'r argae yn rheoli llif yr afon.
english: The dam controls the river flow.
tip: Welsh normally shows ‘of’ by word order, not a separate word: ‘llif yr afon’ = the flow of the river, literally flow the river, with ‘yr’ on the last noun.

target: Dechreuais i ddysgu Cymraeg.
english: I started learning Welsh.
tip: The object after a past-tense verb softens its first word: ‘dysgu’ becomes ‘ddysgu’ after ‘dechreuais i’ (I started).

target: Daethon nhw o Loegr.
english: They came from England.
tip: After ‘o’ (from), the sound softens ‘Ll’ to ‘L’: ‘Lloegr’ becomes ‘Loegr’ in ‘o Loegr’.

target: Cyfarfûm i â'r rheolwr.
english: I met the manager.
tip: The ending ‘-ûm’ is a literary past ‘I’. ‘cyfarfûm i’ (I met) is more formal than spoken ‘cwrddais i’.

target: Bwytais i gawl blasus.
english: I ate tasty cawl.
tip: Adjectives normally follow the noun in Welsh: ‘cawl blasus’ is literally soup tasty, for tasty soup.

target: Mae parcio'n anodd yma.
english: Parking is difficult here.
tip: A verb-noun can be the subject, like the English -ing form: ‘parcio’ means parking in ‘mae parcio'n anodd’.

target: Ga i ddefnyddio'r ffôn?
english: May I use the phone?
tip: ‘ga i...?’ asks may I and softens the next verb: ‘defnyddio’ becomes ‘ddefnyddio’.

target: Est ti i'r parti?
english: Did you go to the party?
tip: ‘mynd’ is irregular in the past: ‘est ti’ means you went, as in ‘est ti i'r parti’ (did you go to the party).

target: Owain wnaeth ffeindio'r ci coll.
english: It was Owain who found the lost dog.
tip: Putting the subject first with ‘wnaeth’ adds emphasis: ‘Owain wnaeth ffeindio’ means it was Owain who found.

target: Rhaid i mi gofio prynu bara.
english: I must remember to buy bread.
tip: After ‘rhaid i’ + a person, the verb softens: ‘cofio’ becomes ‘gofio’ in ‘rhaid i mi gofio’.

target: Hoffwn i gael paned o de.
english: I would like to have a cup of tea.
tip: The ‘-wn i’ ending is the would form: ‘hoffwn i’ means I would like, gentler than saying I want.

target: Alli di fy helpu i gyda hyn?
english: Can you help me with this?
tip: The object me wraps the verb as ‘fy...i’: ‘fy helpu i’ means help me in ‘alli di fy helpu i’.

target: Roedd hi'n arfer byw ger y môr.
english: She used to live near the sea.
tip: ‘arfer’ after ‘roedd’ means used to, for past habits: ‘roedd hi'n arfer byw’ is she used to live.

target: Diolchodd hi i'r meddyg am y cymorth.
english: She thanked the doctor for the help.
tip: You thank to someone in Welsh: ‘diolch’ takes ‘i’, so ‘diolchodd hi i'r meddyg’ is she thanked the doctor.

target: Rhaid iddi hi dalu'r bil cyn dydd Gwener.
english: She must pay the bill before Friday.
tip: To her contracts to ‘iddi’, and the verb softens: ‘talu’ becomes ‘dalu’ in ‘rhaid iddi hi dalu’.

target: Os doi di'n gynnar, gallwn ni gael coffi.
english: If you come early, we can have coffee.
tip: After ‘os’ (if), the present ‘doi di’ covers the future: ‘os doi di'n gynnar’ means if you come early.

target: Roedd e'n gweithio yn y swyddfa pan ffoniais i.
english: He was working in the office when I called.
tip: ‘roedd e'n gweithio’ (was working) is the ongoing background, and the ‘-ais’ past ‘ffoniais i’ marks the one-off event.

target: Gofynnodd y meddyg a oeddwn i'n cymryd unrhyw foddion.
english: The doctor asked if I was taking any medication.
tip: Indirect yes/no questions use ‘a’ for whether: ‘gofynnodd... a oeddwn i’ means asked if I was.

target: Dylwn i fod wedi edrych ar y tywydd yn gyntaf.
english: I should have checked the weather first.
tip: I should have is ‘dylwn i fod wedi’ + a verb: ‘dylwn i fod wedi edrych’ means I should have looked.

target: Roedd angen seibiant arna i ar ôl yr holl waith.
english: I needed a break after all that work.
tip: Need is felt on you in Welsh: ‘angen... arna i’ means I need, so ‘roedd angen... arna i’ is I needed.
